text:
In spite of myself, I glanced at the bed; it had not been disturbed. As for Marguerite, she was already wearing a white dressing gown.

We sat down at the table.

Charm, gentleness, openness—Marguerite had everything, and from time to time I was forced to acknowledge that I had no right to ask anything more of her; that many people would have been happy in my place, and that, like Virgil’s shepherd, I had only to enjoy the leisure that a god—or rather, a goddess—was granting me.

I tried to put Prudence’s theories into practice and to be as cheerful as my two companions; but what came naturally to them was an effort for me, and the nervous laughter by which they were deceived came very close to tears.

At last supper ended, and I was left alone with Marguerite. As was her custom, she went and sat on her rug before the fire and gazed sadly at the flame in the hearth.

She was thinking! Of what? I do not know; for my part, I watched her with love and almost with terror as I thought of what I was ready to suffer for her.

“Knowest thou what I was thinking about?”

“No.”

“About a plan I have devised.”

“And what is this plan?”

“I cannot confide it to thee yet, but I can tell thee what would result from it. The result would be that a month from now I should be free, I should no longer owe anything, and we should go and spend the summer together in the country.”

“And you cannot tell me by what means?”

“No; thou needst only love me as I love thee, and everything will succeed.”

“And did you devise this plan all by yourself?”

“Yes.”

“And will you carry it out alone?”

“I alone shall have the troubles,” Marguerite said to me with a smile I shall never forget, “but we shall share the profits.”

I could not help blushing at the word profits; I remembered Manon Lescaut and Des Grieux living on M. de B.’s money.

I replied in a somewhat harsh tone as I rose:

“You will permit me, my dear Marguerite, to share only in the profits of ventures that I devise and conduct myself.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means that I strongly suspect Monsieur le Comte de G. of being your partner in this fortunate plan, whose liabilities and profits alike I decline to share.”

“You are a child. I thought you loved me; I was mistaken. Very well.”

At the same time, she rose, opened her piano, and began once more to play the Invitation to the Dance, up to that famous passage in the major key at which she always stopped.

Was it out of habit, or to remind me of the day when we had met? All I know is that the melody brought my memories back, and, going up to her, I took her head between my hands and kissed her.

“Do you forgive me?” I said to her.

“You can see that I do,” she replied; “but bear in mind that this is only our second day, and already I have something to forgive you for. You keep your promises of blind obedience very poorly.”

“What do you expect, Marguerite? I love you too much, and I am jealous of your slightest thought. What you proposed to me just now would drive me mad with joy, but the mystery preceding the execution of this plan constricts my heart.”

“Come, let us reason a little,” she resumed, taking both my hands and looking at me with a charming smile that I found it impossible to resist. “You love me, do you not? And you would be happy to spend three or four months in the country alone with me. I too should be happy in that solitude together; not only should I be happy in it, but I need it for my health. I cannot leave Paris for so long without putting my affairs in order, and the affairs of a woman like me are always very tangled. Well, I have found a way to reconcile everything—my affairs and my love for you; yes, for you, do not laugh: I am mad enough to love you! And now you put on your grand airs and make grand pronouncements to me. Child, child three times over, remember only that I love you, and do not worry about anything. Is it agreed, then?”

“Whatever you wish is agreed; you know that very well.”

“Then, within a month, we shall be in some village, strolling along the water’s edge and drinking milk. It seems strange to you to hear me speak this way, me, Marguerite Gautier. It is because, my friend, when this Parisian life, which seems to make me so happy, is not burning me, it wearies me, and then I am suddenly filled with longings for a calmer existence that would remind me of my childhood. One has always had a childhood, whatever one may have become. Oh, do not worry; I am not going to tell you that I am the daughter of a retired colonel and that I was educated at Saint-Denis. I am a poor country girl, and six years ago I did not know how to write my own name. You are reassured now, are you not? Why are you the first person to whom I turn to share the joy of the longing that has come over me? No doubt because I recognized that you loved me for myself and not for yourself, whereas the others have never loved me except for themselves.

“I have very often been to the country, but never as I should have liked to go. I am counting on you for this simple happiness, so do not be unkind; grant it to me. Tell yourself this: she is not destined to live to old age, and one day I should regret not having done for her the first thing she asked of me, when it was so easy to do.”

What could one reply to such words, especially with the memory of a first night of love and in anticipation of a second?

An hour later, I held Marguerite in my arms, and had she asked me to commit a crime, I would have obeyed her.

At six in the morning I left, and before leaving I said to her:

“Tonight?”

She kissed me more tightly, but did not answer.

During the day, I received a letter containing these words:

“Dear child, I am a little unwell, and the doctor has ordered me to rest. I shall go to bed early tonight and shall not see you. But, to reward you, I shall expect you tomorrow at noon. I love you.”
